Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantavirus Disease in a Changing World: Reservoir Ecology, Endothelial Dysfunction, Clinical Management, and the 2026 M/V Hondius Andes Virus Outbreak
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses maintained in diverse mammalian reservoirs. Human disease is caused predominantly by orthohantaviruses and manifests chiefly as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia or hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS) in the Americas. Andes virus (ANDV) is epidemiologically distinctive because limited human-to-human transmission has been repeatedly documented. This update-oriented narrative review synthesizes evidence available through to 28 August 2026 and is organized around an integrative framework linking reservoir ecology and spillover, ANDV-specific person-to-person transmission, endothelial and immune dysfunction, clinical phenotype, critical-care management, and One Health preparedness. The recent 2026 M/V Hondius outbreak is used as a case study of how a primarily rodent-borne infection can generate international operational consequences in a mobile, closed setting. Recent HFRS surveillance from Asia and Europe is included to balance the ANDV-focused outbreak analysis. Severe disease is associated with endothelial barrier dysfunction, capillary leak, thrombocytopenia, myocardial or renal involvement, and dysregulated host responses rather than widespread endothelial necrosis. Current evidence supports early recognition and organ support; evidence for ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed vascular therapies differs substantially by syndrome and remains limited or investigational for HPS/HCPS. The M/V Hondius event ultimately involved 13 cases (12 confirmed and one probable) and three deaths, with no further secondary cases after completion of international follow-up.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic, tri‑segmented negative‑sense RNA viruses maintained in diverse mammalian reservoirs, causing HFRS in Eurasia and HPS/HCPS in the Americas.
analysis.main_directions: The review is organized around an integrative framework linking reservoir ecology and spillover, ANDV‑specific person‑to‑person transmission, endothelial and immune dysfunction, clinical phenotype, critical‑care management, and One Health preparedness.
analysis.current_state: Severe disease is associated with endothelial barrier dysfunction, capillary leak, and dysregulated host responses; early recognition and organ support are supported, while evidence for ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, and host‑directed vascular therapies remains limited or investigational for HPS/HCPS.
analysis.gaps: Therapeutic evidence is sparse and heterogeneous, and the mechanisms underlying limited human‑to‑human transmission of ANDV are not fully resolved.
analysis.future_research: Rigorous clinical trials of ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, and vascular‑targeted therapies, together with enhanced surveillance of ANDV transmission dynamics, are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses with diverse mammalian reservoirs, causing HFRS in Eurasia and HPS/HCPS in the Americas. Main directions: The review integrates reservoir ecology, ANDV person‑to‑person transmission, endothelial dysfunction, clinical phenotype, critical‑care management, and One Health preparedness, using the 2026 M/V Hondius outbreak as a case study. Current state: Severe disease involves endothelial barrier dysfunction and dysregulated host responses; early recognition and organ support are beneficial, but therapeutic options remain limited or investigational. Gaps: Evidence for specific antivirals and host‑directed treatments is sparse, and ANDV transmission mechanisms are incompletely understood. Future research: Conduct rigorous trials of ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, and vascular‑targeted agents, and strengthen surveillance of ANDV spillover and person‑to‑person spread.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是人畜共患的三段负链RNA病毒,维持在多样的哺乳动物宿主中,可导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热和美洲的汉坦病毒肺综合征/汉坦病毒心肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述围绕一个整合框架组织,链接宿主生态与溢出、安第斯病毒特异性的人际传播、内皮和免疫功能失调、临床表型、危重症管理以及One Health准备。
analysis_zh.current_state: 严重疾病与内皮屏障功能障碍、毛细血管漏出以及宿主反应失调相关;早期识别和器官支持得到支持,但针对汉坦病毒肺综合征/汉坦病毒心肺综合征的利巴韦林、免疫血浆、单克隆抗体以及针对宿主的血管治疗的证据仍然有限或处于研究阶段。
analysis_zh.gaps: 治疗证据稀缺且异质,且安第斯病毒有限的人际传播机制尚未完全阐明。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要开展严格的利巴韦林、免疫血浆、单克隆抗体和血管靶向疗法的临床试验,并加强对安第斯病毒传播动态的监测。

papers.title: Hantavirus infection and the boundaries of autoimmunity: Vascular immunopathology, autoimmune-like mimicry, and post-infectious phenomena.
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses causing acute systemic vascular syndromes, principally haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although primarily infectious, hantavirus disease may generate vascular, renal, haematological, and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune-mediated disorders. This Review critically examines the boundary between infection-driven immunopathology and autoimmunity. Hantavirus infection involves endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine and chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis, and adaptive immune responses, whose expression is further influenced by virus-, host-, and tissue-specific factors. These mechanisms contribute to the marked heterogeneity of clinical disease and may reproduce autoimmune-like clinical and laboratory features, but do not, in themselves, establish sustained loss of immune tolerance. Current evidence is substantially stronger for acute infection-associated immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry than for persistent autoreactivity or causally attributable post-infectious autoimmune disease. Reported autoimmune phenomena remain uncommon and predominantly case-based, while longitudinal, antigen-specific, and epidemiological evidence is limited. Persistent or recurrent manifestations after resolution of infection therefore require additional serological, histopathological, or other objective evidence of sustained immune dysregulation. Hantavirus infection thus provides a clinically informative model for distinguishing antiviral immunopathology from autoimmune-like mimicry and rare possible post-infectious autoimmunity, with direct implications for diagnosis and therapeutic restraint. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES.

source_records.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses causing acute systemic vascular syndromes, principally haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although primarily infectious, hantavirus disease may generate vascular, renal, haematological, and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune-mediated disorders. This Review critically examines the boundary between infection-driven immunopathology and autoimmunity. Hantavirus infection involves endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine and chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis, and adaptive immune responses, whose expression is further influenced by virus-, host-, and tissue-specific factors. These mechanisms contribute to the marked heterogeneity of clinical disease and may reproduce autoimmune-like clinical and laboratory features, but do not, in themselves, establish sustained loss of immune tolerance. Current evidence is substantially stronger for acute infection-associated immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry than for persistent autoreactivity or causally attributable post-infectious autoimmune disease. Reported autoimmune phenomena remain uncommon and predominantly case-based, while longitudinal, antigen-specific, and epidemiological evidence is limited. Persistent or recurrent manifestations after resolution of infection therefore require additional serological, histopathological, or other objective evidence of sustained immune dysregulation. Hantavirus infection thus provides a clinically informative model for distinguishing antiviral immunopathology from autoimmune-like mimicry and rare possible post-infectious autoimmunity, with direct implications for diagnosis and therapeutic restraint. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES.

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物携带的RNA病毒,导致急性全身血管综合征,促使研究其与免疫介导性疾病的重叠。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了内皮功能障碍、先天抗病毒感知、干扰素、细胞因子/趋化因子放大、补体活化、免疫血栓形成及适应性免疫等机制,这些机制可产生自身免疫样的临床和实验室特征。

papers.title: A single-amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and can be transmitted person‑to‑person, making its transmission mechanisms clinically important.
analysis.methods: A human ANDV isolate from a person‑to‑person outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region were compared for lethality in Syrian golden hamsters; genomic sequencing identified mutations; strand‑specific RT‑qPCR measured viral RNA synthesis; and human cell expression systems examined glycoprotein trafficking and virion‑like particle release.
analysis.results: Sequencing revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including a T641I change in the glycoprotein precursor; the human isolate showed delayed virion release despite similar RNA synthesis; introducing the reciprocal I641T mutation in human cells decreased Golgi retention and accelerated release of virus‑like particles.
analysis.contribution: The T641I substitution is suggested to be a human‑adaptive mutation that modifies glycoprotein trafficking and enhances viral egress, providing a mechanistic clue to factors that may facilitate person‑to‑person spread of ANDV.
analysis.limitations: The summary is based only on abstract information; detailed methods, sample sizes, statistical analyses, and broader experimental context are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and can spread person-to-person, raising public‑health concerns. Methods: Human and rodent ANDV isolates were compared for hamster lethality, sequenced, analyzed by strand‑specific RT‑qPCR, and expressed in human cells to study glycoprotein trafficking. Results: Twenty‑five nonsynonymous mutations were found, notably T641I in the glycoprotein; the human isolate showed delayed virion release despite similar RNA synthesis, and the I641T revertant reduced Golgi retention and sped particle release. Contribution: The T641I change may represent a human‑adaptive mutation affecting glycoprotein trafficking and virus egress, informing understanding of transmissibility. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed experimental parameters and statistical analyses are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 啮齿动物与人类之间的单个氨基酸差异 安第斯病毒 影响病毒糖蛋白的运输。

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒(ANDV))导致汉坦病毒肺综合征,且可人际传播,使其传播机制在临床上具有重要意义。
analysis_zh.methods: 将来自人际传播暴发的安第斯病毒(ANDV)人源分离株与同一区域的啮齿动物分离株在叙利亚金仓鼠中比较致死性;通过基因组测序鉴定突变;使用链特异性RT‐qPCR测定病毒RNA合成;并利用人细胞表达系统研究糖蛋白的转运及类病毒颗粒的释放。
analysis_zh.results: 测序发现25个非同义置换,其中包括糖蛋白前体的T641I突变;尽管RNA合成相似,人源分离株表现出病毒释放延迟;在人体细胞中引入相反的I641T突变可降低高尔基体滞留并加速类病毒颗粒的释放。
analysis_zh.contribution: T641I置换被认为是一种人源适应性突变,可改变糖蛋白转运并增强病毒外排,为可能促进安第斯病毒(ANDV)人际传播的因素提供了机制线索。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本摘要仅基于摘要信息;未报告详细方法、样本量、统计分析及更广泛的实验背景。

papers.title: Hantavirus Outbreak Caused by Andes Virus Linked to International Cruise Ship Travel - United States, 2026.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV), the only hantavirus known to be transmitted person-to-person, is endemic to areas of South America and can cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, which has a case-fatality rate of approximately 40%. On May 4, 2026, CDC was notified of seven cases of severe acute respiratory illness, including three deaths, among 147 persons aboard a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean; the illnesses were later confirmed to be caused by ANDV. No cases occurred among passengers who were U.S. residents. Ten of 28 U.S. resident passengers disembarked before ANDV infection was confirmed aboard the ship. On May 10, the remaining 18 U.S. resident passengers were repatriated to the National Quarantine Unit in Omaha, Nebraska, for risk assessment and monitoring, and where optimized advanced care was available, should symptoms develop. CDC and U.S. health departments monitored 60 additional U.S. residents potentially exposed on flights involving a passenger with symptomatic ANDV infection from the cruise, totaling 88 contacts across 27 jurisdictions. All 88 contacts completed 42 days of monitoring, with no secondary ANDV infections identified. Worldwide, local health authorities assessed and monitored approximately 653 potentially exposed persons from 33 countries. This response highlights the value of rapid coordination among partners to locate and monitor potentially exposed persons during an international outbreak to reduce the risk for ANDV transmission. Prompt notification to public health authorities can facilitate testing, patient care, contact identification, and implementation of measures to limit secondary transmission.

analysis.methods: CDC was notified on 4 May 2026 of seven severe acute respiratory illness cases (including three deaths) among 147 cruise‑ship passengers; illnesses were confirmed as ANDV; 18 U.S. resident passengers were repatriated for risk assessment and monitoring; health departments monitored 60 additional U.S. residents and 88 contacts across 27 jurisdictions for 42 days.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus is the only hantavirus transmitted person‑to‑person, endemic to South America, causing pulmonary syndrome with ~40% fatality. Methods: CDC identified seven severe cases (three deaths) among 147 cruise‑ship passengers on 4 May 2026, confirmed ANDV, repatriated 18 U.S. residents, and monitored 60 additional U.S. residents and 88 contacts across 27 jurisdictions for 42 days. Results: Seven cases were ANDV‑positive; no secondary infections occurred among 88 contacts; ~653 exposed persons from 33 countries were assessed worldwide. Contribution: The investigation demonstrates the importance of rapid inter‑agency coordination and monitoring to limit secondary transmission. Limitations: Only an abstract is available, limiting detail on methods and data.

papers.title: Progress in antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus: Current advances and future perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-associated zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), two clinically distinct diseases characterized by vascular dysfunction and potentially severe organ failure. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, and recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. This review highlights the experimental and clinical evidence needed to advance promising antiviral and vaccine candidates toward effective strategies for prevention and treatment of hantavirus infections.

Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 2 of 23 Narrative Review Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, tripartite, negative-sense RNA viruses within the family Hantaviridae. The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. Recent surveillance data illustrate the continuing, geographically heterogeneous disease burden. In China, national surveillance recorded 3,271 cases of epidemic hemorrhagic fever and 16 deaths in 2025 [17]. In the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA), 1,885 hantavirus infections were reported in 2023, corresponding to a notification rate of 0.4 cases per 100,000 population [18]. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 229 confirmed cases of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and 59 deaths through epidemiological week 47 of 2025, corresponding to a reported case-fatality proportion of 25.7% [19]. These figures originate from different years, surveillance systems, and case definitions and should not be interpreted as directly comparable estimates of regional incidence or disease lethality. Despite this burden, supportive management remains the cornerstone of clinical care, and no antiviral has demonstrated consistent efficacy across HFRS and HCPS [9]. A randomized clinical trial conducted in China reported reduced mortality and selected complications among patients with HFRS receiving intravenous ribavirin [20]. However, a placebo-controlled trial in HCPS did not establish a clinical benefit during the cardiopulmonary phase, underscoring why treatment findings cannot be generalized across syndromes or disease stages [21]. Favipiravir has shown antiviral activity and improved survival under selected preclinical conditions [22]. RNA interference has suppressed Andes virus replication in cultured cells [23]. Neutralizing monoclonal antibodies have conferred protection in selected animal challenge models, but their efficacy in patients remains unconfirmed [24]. Collectively, these findings illustrate the different levels of evidence supporting current antiviral candidates, ranging from clinical investigation to in vitro and animal-model studies [25]. Prevention faces similar translational challenges. Inactivated vaccines targeting HFRS- associated hantaviruses have been implemented in China [26], while Hantavax is an authorized Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 3 of 23 Narrative Review inactivated Hantaan virus vaccine in South Korea [27]. In contrast, a bivalent Hantaan/Puumala DNA vaccine has reached phase IIa clinical evaluation for safety and immunogenicity, without demonstrating clinical effectiveness against naturally acquired infection [28]. Recombinant protein, viral vector-based, and messenger RNA vaccine platforms have been investigated predominantly in preclinical studies, and the breadth and durability of vaccine-induced protection remain important evidence gaps [29]. Accordingly, the aim of this narrative review is to critically evaluate the molecular rationale, evidence levels, and translational limitations of current hantavirus antiviral and vaccine strategies. The discussion first summarizes mechanisms relevant to therapeutic targeting and antigen design, then compares clinically investigated interventions with preclinical and exploratory approaches, assesses the development status of vaccine platforms, and identifies priorities for further experimental and clinical validation. Virology and pathogenesis of hantavirus Genome organization and viral structure The hantavirus genome comprises three RNA segments, each encoding proteins with distinct roles in the viral life cycle. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA and participates in viral RNA synthesis [1]. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which mediate viral attachment and membrane fusion [30]. Because Gn and Gc contain neutralizing antibody epitopes, they represent important targets for antibody-based interventions and vaccine antigen design [31−33]. Furthermore, the ability of Gn and Gc to self-assemble into virus-like particles in experimental expression systems provides a potential platform for vaccine antigen presentation [34]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is responsible for viral messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication [1]. During transcription, the viral transcription machinery uses short capped RNA primers acquired from host transcripts through cap-snatching to synthesize mRNA from negative-sense genomic RNA (vRNA) [35]. In contrast, genome replication proceeds through primer-independent synthesis of a full-length positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA), or antigenome, from the vRNA template [36]. The antigenome subsequently serves as an intermediate template for producing new negative-sense genomic RNA, rather than functioning as a protein-coding transcript [37]. These mechanistically distinct steps identify RdRp and viral RNA synthesis as relevant targets for direct-acting antivirals. In addition, experimental evidence demonstrating interactions between N and RdRp highlights the importance of the viral replication complex in RNA synthesis [38]. Viral entry and host interaction Hantavirus entry begins with Gn/Gc-mediated interactions with host-cell entry factors, followed by endocytosis and membrane fusion within endosomal compartments [13,30]. Earlier cell-based studies implicated αvβ3 integrins in entry by certain HFRS-associated hantaviruses [39]. In contrast, protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been experimentally identified as a critical entry factor for Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus in pulmonary endothelial cells. Disruption of PCDH1 expression also conferred protection against Andes virus challenge in hamsters [40]. These findings indicate that entry-factor dependence differs among hantaviruses and should not be represented as a single universal receptor pathway. For Hantaan virus, clathrin-dependent receptor-mediated endocytosis was demonstrated in a cell-based investigation, although this pathway should not be assumed to operate identically in all hantaviruses [41]. Gn and Gc contribute complementary functions to viral attachment, membrane fusion, and virion assembly [42]. Following entry, pathogenic hantaviruses primarily target vascular endothelial cells, where infection can impair barrier function without extensive direct viral cytolysis [13]. Experimental studies have linked enhanced vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling to increased endothelial permeability [14]. Specifically, Andes virus infection of human lung endothelial cells has been associated with increased VEGF production and reduced junctional VE-cadherin, Khairullah et al. The resulting vascular leakage contributes to renal involvement in HFRS and pulmonary and cardiovascular complications in HCPS [4, 5, 44]. Immunopathogenesis Host immune responses contribute to both control of hantavirus infection and the development of vascular injury. Innate recognition involving retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors activates type I interferon signaling and restricts Hantaan virus replication in experimental systems [46]. However, hantaviruses can modulate these antiviral pathways, and the outcome reflects interactions between viral replication and host immune regulation [37]. In a Hantaan virus model, viral interference with TRIM25-associated RIG-I-like receptor signaling was reported as a mechanism of innate immune antagonism [47]. In an endothelial-cell culture model, hantavirus-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes increased permeability of infected endothelial monolayers, suggesting a potential mechanism of immune-mediated endothelial injury [49]. However, the extent to which this experimental mechanism contributes to vascular pathology in patients remains incompletely established. Dysregulated inflammatory mediators and VEGF- associated signaling may further impair endothelial junctions and amplify vascular leakage [14,15, 50]. These findings highlight the need to distinguish protective antiviral immunity from potentially harmful immune-mediated responses and support the investigation of Khairullah et al. analysis.current_state: Clinical evidence exists for ribavirin and some inactivated vaccines, whereas most other antivirals and novel vaccine candidates remain pre‑clinical or in early‑phase trials with limited human efficacy data. (A4, A5)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe HFRS and HCPS and their diverse geography and antigenic variation hinder countermeasure development. Main directions: Antiviral options (ribavirin, favipiravir, RNAi, monoclonal antibodies, host‑directed therapies) and vaccine platforms (inactivated, DNA, recombinant protein, viral‑vector, mRNA) are reviewed. Current state: Ribavirin and some inactivated vaccines have clinical data; most other antivirals and novel vaccines are pre‑clinical or early‑phase. Gaps: Translation is limited by virus‑specific responses, narrow windows, delivery issues, antigenic diversity, and lack of protective immunity correlates. Future research: Priorities include clinical efficacy trials, defining immune correlates, optimizing delivery, and advancing leading candidates.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Profiling of Human Type II Alveolar Epithelial Cells Following Hantaan Virus Infection
papers.abstract: This study investigated the transcriptional responses of early-passage human type II alveolar epithelial cells (AEC II) following Hantaan virus (HTNV) exposure. RNA sequencing was performed on HTNV-exposed and mock-treated AEC II at 48 hours, with three independent biological replicates per group. The analysis focused on host transcriptional responses, particularly innate immunity, interferon-related signaling, and inflammatory pathways. Study design: Six Homo sapiens samples derived from in vitro cultured human type II alveolar epithelial cells, comprising three independent biological replicates in the HTNV-exposed group and three in the mock-treated control group. Samples were collected at 48 hours after exposure or corresponding mock treatment. Sample collection year: 2022; setting: laboratory. Library strategy: RNA-Seq. Library source: TRANSCRIPTOMIC. Sequencing service provider: Shanghai NovelBio Bio-Pharm Technology, Shanghai, China. Sequencing metadata documented in the supplied method file: Illumina NovaSeq 6000; 150 bp paired-end reads; poly(A) enrichment; TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit. Human reference annotation: GRCh38.p13, as labeled in the expression workbooks. Dataset contents: Processed RNA-seq results, including gene counts, FPKM and TPM expression matrices, quality-control summaries, mapping statistics, differential-expression results, GO and pathway analysis results, plots and original documentation. The six sample identifiers are HTNV-1, HTNV-2, HTNV-3, MOCK-1, MOCK-2 and MOCK-3. No raw FASTQ/FQ, BAM/CRAM or SRA files are included in the supplied archive. The original results archive is preserved without internal modification; English sample metadata and an English README accompany it. Contact: Kaixuan Zhang, Department of Clinical Laboratory, General Hospital of Wanbei Coal and Electricity Group, Yongqiao District, Suzhou, Anhui 235000, China. Email: 2461539536@qq.com.

papers.title: Abstract 14113: The Window Before Collapse: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Introduction: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but devastating cause of acute viral cardiopulmonary failure. While extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is increasingly employed in severe disease, contemporary evidence remains sparse and largely confined to small institutional cohorts. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to define survival and clinical outcomes among ECMO-supported HCPS patients. Methods: This prospectively registered systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD420261416336 ) searched PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar from inception through May 2026. Observational studies and case series were included. Quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Survival to hospital discharge was pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, while ECMO candidacy criteria, deployment strategies, complications, healthcare utilization, and long-term outcomes were qualitatively synthesized. Results: Eight studies met inclusion criteria. Three independent cohorts contributed to quantitative synthesis, yielding a pooled analysis of 71 ECMO-supported patients , a substantial evidence base for a disease in which institutional experience is often limited to single-digit cases. Overall survival following ECMO was 70.4% (50/71; 95% CI 58.9-79.9%; P<0.001) . A striking temporal improvement emerged across three decades of practice, with survival increasing from 14/26 (53.8%) in the earliest cohort to 20/25 (80.0%) and 14/17 (82.3%) in contemporary series. Survival gains paralleled a shift from rescue ECMO to earlier physiology-guided initiation. Even among survivors, recovery remained resource-intensive, requiring mean ECMO support of 127.35 hours. and mean hospital stays of 23.4 days . Major complications included bleeding, limb ischemia, vascular injury, and amputation. Long-term follow-up demonstrated substantial post-discharge morbidity despite survival. Collectively, the literature suggests that improved HCPS outcomes have paralleled a transition from salvage ECMO to a planned physiology-guided strategy, while revealing a significant survivorship burden beyond hospital discharge. Conclusions: HCPS has traditionally been defined by the moment of catastrophic cardiopulmonary collapse. Our findings suggest it may be determined by what happens before it. The consistent improvement in survival observed across successive ECMO eras points toward early recognition of physiologic decline and progressively earlier deployment of mechanical circulatory support as a potentially modifiable determinant of outcome. In a disease measured in hours rather than days, the most important ECMO decision may not be how to run it—but when to start it.

In a disease measured in hours rather than days, the most important ECMO decision may not be how to run it—but when to start it.

source_records.title: Abstract 14113: The Window Before Collapse: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
source_records.abstract: Introduction: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but devastating cause of acute viral cardiopulmonary failure. While extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is increasingly employed in severe disease, contemporary evidence remains sparse and largely confined to small institutional cohorts. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to define survival and clinical outcomes among ECMO-supported HCPS patients. Methods: This prospectively registered systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD420261416336 ) searched PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar from inception through May 2026. Observational studies and case series were included. Quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Survival to hospital discharge was pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, while ECMO candidacy criteria, deployment strategies, complications, healthcare utilization, and long-term outcomes were qualitatively synthesized. Results: Eight studies met inclusion criteria. Three independent cohorts contributed to quantitative synthesis, yielding a pooled analysis of 71 ECMO-supported patients , a substantial evidence base for a disease in which institutional experience is often limited to single-digit cases. Overall survival following ECMO was 70.4% (50/71; 95% CI 58.9-79.9%; P<0.001) . A striking temporal improvement emerged across three decades of practice, with survival increasing from 14/26 (53.8%) in the earliest cohort to 20/25 (80.0%) and 14/17 (82.3%) in contemporary series. Survival gains paralleled a shift from rescue ECMO to earlier physiology-guided initiation. Even among survivors, recovery remained resource-intensive, requiring mean ECMO support of 127.35 hours. and mean hospital stays of 23.4 days . Major complications included bleeding, limb ischemia, vascular injury, and amputation. Long-term follow-up demonstrated substantial post-discharge morbidity despite survival. Collectively, the literature suggests that improved HCPS outcomes have paralleled a transition from salvage ECMO to a planned physiology-guided strategy, while revealing a significant survivorship burden beyond hospital discharge. Conclusions: HCPS has traditionally been defined by the moment of catastrophic cardiopulmonary collapse. Our findings suggest it may be determined by what happens before it. The consistent improvement in survival observed across successive ECMO eras points toward early recognition of physiologic decline and progressively earlier deployment of mechanical circulatory support as a potentially modifiable determinant of outcome. In a disease measured in hours rather than days, the most important ECMO decision may not be how to run it—but when to start it.

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8 + T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8 + regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8 + Tregs (CD122 + Eomes + CD49d lo KIR + ), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8 + Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8 + T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8 + Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8 + Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8 + Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis.background: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology (A1).
analysis.methods: The study characterized an HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ regulatory T‑cell (Treg) subset in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model (A2), and performed immunization with identified Qa‑1‑binding HTNV peptides followed by viral challenge (A5).
analysis.results: CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+) were markedly reduced in patient blood and displayed a terminally differentiated phenotype (high KLRG‑1, NKG2A, CTLA‑4, Fas‑L) correlating with disease severity (A3); WT mice immunized with these peptides showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock‑in mice cleared virus better but had exacerbated pathology (A5); Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Tregs suppressed effector CD8+ proliferation in a peptide‑specific, TGF‑β‑dependent manner (A6); the D227K mutation altered Treg phenotype and reduced antigen‑specific suppressive function (A7); overall, these Tregs restrain immunopathology at the cost of delayed viral elimination (A8).
analysis.contribution: The findings identify HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Tregs as modulators that limit immunopathology during HTNV infection, suggesting a therapeutic axis for HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers (A9).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is provided; detailed methods, sample sizes, and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV causes HFRS where CD8+ T cells drive clearance and immunopathology. Methods: Researchers characterized an HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Treg subset in patients and a murine HTNV model, including peptide immunization and challenge. Results: CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+) were reduced in patients, showed terminal differentiation (high KLRG‑1, NKG2A, CTLA‑4, Fas‑L) correlating with severity; WT mice immunized with Qa‑1‑binding peptides had less renal pathology, while D227K mice cleared virus better but had increased pathology; these Tregs suppressed effector CD8+ proliferation via peptide‑specific, TGF‑β‑dependent mechanisms, and the D227K mutation altered their phenotype and function. Contribution: Demonstrates that HLA‑E/Qa‑1‑restricted CD8+ Tregs curb immunopathology at the expense of delayed viral clearance, offering a therapeutic target for HFRS. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed experimental information is not reported.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of serological, molecular and rapid tests for human hantavirus disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human hantavirus disease is potentially lethal and overlaps clinically with other febrile, renal, and cardiopulmonary syndromes. Diagnostic performance varies by viral species, specimen type, sampling timing, and reference standard. OBJECTIVE: To synthesize and compare the diagnostic accuracy of serologic, molecular, rapid, multiplex, and antigen-detection tests for human hantavirus infection or disease. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261398030). MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through May 20, 2026. Human studies with an eligible index test and verifiable reference standard were included. Diagnostic accuracy data were extracted when possible. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2 and certainty with GRADE-DTA. Primary meta-analyses used platform-specific univariate logit-scale models; hierarchical bivariate/HSROC sensitivity analyses were performed for eligible strata. RESULTS: Sixty-three studies were included; 24 contributed 2 × 2 data and 22 primary comparisons entered the main synthesis. ELISA/EIA showed sensitivity of 98.0% and specificity of 98.8%, with low certainty. Rapid-format assays showed sensitivity of 97.4% and specificity of 97.2%, also with low certainty. Molecular tests had specificity of 99.5% and sensitivity of 85.6%. Bivariate sensitivity analyses for ELISA/EIA and rapid-format assays produced similar estimates to the primary models. CONCLUSIONS: In the available low-certainty evidence, ELISA/EIA serology is the best-supported platform, but this is not a universal recommendation. Molecular and rapid tests may be useful in specific contexts and require prospective validation.

papers.title: Dinámica de la Información Digital en español ante un riesgo emergente de salud pública: análisis exploratorio del caso hantavirus
papers.abstract: Este artículo analiza la dinámica temporal de la información digital en español relacionada con el hantavirus como caso de un riesgo emergente de salud pública. Se realizó un estudio observacional, retrospectivo, descriptivo y exploratorio a partir de publicaciones digitales recuperadas mediante un canal de monitoreo orientado a México. De las 1,054 publicaciones en español recuperadas, 899 conformaron el corpus final, correspondiente al periodo del 7 de mayo al 8 de agosto de 2026. La delimitación temporal y la exclusión de registros sin fecha válida definieron esta selección. El volumen de publicaciones se analizó por día y los periodos de mayor actividad se identificaron a partir de la media y la desviación estándar. Se observaron tres episodios principales, con máximos de 78, 139 y 169 publicaciones. Los seis días clasificados como de alta actividad reunieron el 71.5% del corpus. El mayor volumen se registró el 19 de mayo, fecha en la que predominaron los contenidos relacionados con vigilancia o investigación epidemiológica (41.4%). La actividad informativa mostró una clara concentración temporal y una composición distinta entre episodios. Estos patrones permiten caracterizar cómo evolucionó el entorno informativo ante acontecimientos de interés para la salud pública. El volumen de publicaciones, sin embargo, no representa una medida de intensidad epidemiológica.
